claims.text: The initial FeNiCrMn alloy has an FCC structure.
The FeNiCrMn material is a single crystal with a random solid-solution microstructure and no precipitates or secondary phases.
The relevant loading window is 77-600 K and strain rates of 10^-4 to 10^3 s^-1.
Chemical short-range order is present in the target FeNiCrMn alloy.
Severe lattice distortion creates high friction against partial-dislocation motion.
Chemical short-range order creates high Peierls barriers for dislocation motion.
The SRO and lattice-distortion barriers impede partial-dislocation glide more strongly than partial-dislocation nucleation.
Yielding is initiated by thermally activated partial-dislocation nucleation at free surfaces or pre-existing defects.
Bulk dislocation glide is not the process governing the onset of yielding.
A phase transformation is not the process governing the onset of yielding.
At low temperatures and high strain rates, thermal activation of partial-dislocation nucleation remains the dominant mechanism.
High lattice friction prevents newly nucleated dislocations from gliding immediately.
Suppression of immediate dislocation glide produces high yield strength and weak strain-rate sensitivity.
The nucleation barrier is high and relatively temperature-independent in the relevant regime, or the rate-limiting step shifts from glide to nucleation.
Yield strength will depend only weakly on strain rate compared with pure FCC metals.
Yield strength will depend strongly on temperature and exhibit a high activation volume.
Nucleation-controlled yielding will produce a pop-in during nanoindentation or a sharp yield point during tensile testing.
No FCC-to-BCC transformation will occur during initial yielding.
Traditional FCC metals such as Cu and Ni have high strain-rate-sensitive yield strengths because thermally activated glide over short-range obstacles is rate limiting.
Testing both [111] and [001] tensile orientations is required to assess crystal-orientation anisotropy.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as a random solid solution, while the proposed mediator requires chemical short-range ordering. A strictly random solution and substantive SRO are incompatible unless the distinction between average randomness and local order is clarified.

The mechanism describes the controlling nucleation barrier as relatively temperature-independent, whereas the predicted outcome asserts strong temperature dependence. The alternative statement that the rate-limiting process may shift does not resolve which prediction applies.
